---
name: gate-spec
description: >-
  Use this, not a freehand verdict, whenever a spec must be judged ready before planning: "gate this spec", "is this spec ready?", "check this spec before we plan it". Default disposition is fail. Checks the spec on its own terms and returns a verdict@3 with blockers specific enough for scribe/draft-spec to act on.
version: 2.1.0
---

# Scribe — Gate Spec

<overview>
The binding exit gate for a spec entering planning. Delegates to `exit-gate`. On pass, this skill — not the agent — performs the disk-write orchestration below; that step is load-bearing, not decoration. On a retry, pass the gate `retry_count` and the previous round's blockers so it applies the round rules.
</overview>

<dispatch>
| Agent | Model / Effort | Delegate When |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **exit-gate** | opus / high | A spec@1 (after `scribe/verify-spec` and `scribe/audit-spec`) needs a terminal binding pass/fail verdict before planning. |
</dispatch>

<orchestration>
After `exit-gate` returns a pass verdict, THE SKILL SHALL, before handing off to `navigator`:
1. Write the spec@1 JSON to `<workspace_root>/docs/specs/<id>.json`. Create the directory if it does not exist.
2. Commit the file to version control. An uncommitted spec file is invisible to a fresh checkout, a future session, and `scribe/spec-drift` — it exists only in the current working tree.
3. Set `spec_file_path` to the workspace-relative path (e.g. `docs/specs/SPEC-001.json`) in the spec@1 object.
4. Pass the updated spec@1 — with `spec_file_path` set — to `navigator`.

Without `spec_file_path` set, downstream agents fall back to reading the spec from conversation context, which is lossy under compression and cannot be independently verified.

**2-Round Circuit Breaker**: drafter ↔ auditor review loops (via `scribe/draft-spec` and `scribe/audit-spec`) are capped at 2 iterations before reaching this gate. On round 2, unresolved debates about internal helper names or line citations are demoted to non-blocking `api_notes` rather than looping further.
</orchestration>

<references>
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/schemas/spec@1.json`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/schemas/verdict@3.json`
</references>

<io>
**Consumes**: `spec@1` (post-verify, post-audit-spec, post-audit-architecture)
**Produces**: `verdict@3`. On pass, a persisted `spec@1` with `spec_file_path` set, routed to `navigator`. On fail, blockers routed back to `scribe/draft-spec`.
</io>
---
name: audit-architecture
description: >-
  Use when a draft spec@1 should be checked against whole-system architecture before scribe/gate-spec: "check this spec against our architecture", "does this fit the system", "audit this against the arch model". Checks it against the persisted arch-model@2 (building or refreshing it if absent or stale) and returns specific rewritten fixes on fail.
version: 1.0.0
---

# Scribe — Audit Architecture

<overview>
Closes the gap `scribe/audit-spec` leaves open: a spec can be internally consistent — testable criteria, no TBDs, no vague language — and still be wrong for the system it's joining. Delegates to `arch-auditor`. Runs after `scribe/audit-spec` and before `scribe/gate-spec`, so a spec doesn't reach the binding gate without a system-scope check, not just a spec-scope one.
</overview>

<dispatch>
| Agent | Model / Effort | Delegate When |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **arch-auditor** | opus / high | A spec@1 (post `scribe/audit-spec`) needs checking against the workspace's persisted architecture model before `scribe/gate-spec`. Also invoked directly in build mode to construct or refresh the model on demand. |
</dispatch>

<references>
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/schemas/spec@1.json`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/schemas/arch-model@2.json`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/schemas/arch-audit@1.json`

Keep command output and scripts out of the thread as `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/references/tooling/context.md` says.
</references>

<orchestration>
WHEN `arch-auditor` runs in build mode and returns an `arch-model@2`, THE SKILL SHALL write it to `<workspace_root>/docs/architecture/model.json` (creating the directory if absent) and commit it — the model is maintained state, not a per-id gated artifact, so a build/refresh pass overwrites the same file rather than creating a new one. An uncommitted model is invisible to a future session on the s

Check mode produces no disk write of its own — it only reads the existing model.
</orchestration>

<io>
**Consumes**: `spec@1` (post-audit-spec), the persisted `arch-model@2` at `docs/architecture/model.json` if present
**Produces**: `arch-audit@1` in check mode (route to `scribe/gate-spec` on pass, back to `scribe/draft-spec` on fail — same 2-round circuit breaker as `scribe/audit-spec`); `arch-model@2` in build mode, persisted per the orchestration above
</io>

# navigator — Implementation Planning **Stage:** Plan · **Output:** `plan@1` · **Version:** 2.5.0 Decomposes a `spec@1` into a sequenced, testable implementation plan. Every task in `plan@1` is self-contained (see [Task Requirements](#task-requirements)), so an implementer with no domain knowledge can execute it — [smith](../smith/) may still adapt the baseline's shape, provided the same files, criteria, and tests are satisfied. When the spec is corrected after implementation reveals it was wrong, planner runs in amend mode — patching only the affected tasks rather than re-decomposing the wh Once `challenger` passes it, the plan is written to `docs/projects/.json` and committed — the same persistence discipline `scribe` applies to specs, so `weaver/audit-backlog` can check plan coverage, not just spec coverage. One skill, not several — see [Behavior](#behavior) below for how it adapts to the request. --- ## When to Use - You have a `spec@1` and need a concrete, ordered task list before implementation begins - You want to identify which tasks can be parallelized and which have blocking dependencies - You need time estimates for scheduling - You want an adversarial review of a draft plan before handing it to an implementer **Invoke with:** `"Plan the implementation for this spec"`, `"Break this spec into tasks"`, `"What's the implementation order for this?"`, `"Estimate the work in this plan"`, `"Challenge this implementation plan"` --- ## Install **Claude Code** — add the marketplace once, then install by ID: ``` /plugin marketplace add orin-dx/wisp-plugins /plugin install navigator ``` **AGY** — installs the full repo; see the [root README](../../README.md#install) for instructions. **Codex** — see the [root Codex setup](../../README.md#codex), then run `codex plugin add navigator@wisp-plugins`. --- ## Behavior `navigator` is one skill (directory `skills/plan/`), not several — there is no separate `navigator/estimate` or `navigator/challenge` skill to invoke; estimating and challenging both happen inside this one `plan` skill. Behavior adapts to what's asked, dispatching to whichever agent below fits the request: - **Decompose a spec into a plan** → `planner` - **Estimate an existing plan** → `estimator` - **Challenge a draft plan** → `challenger` --- ## Subagents | Subagent | Role | Tier | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `planner` | Planner | sonnet / medium | Decomposes the spec into ordered tasks, grouped into Subsystem Batches by compilation boundary. Also runs in amend mode after a spec correction. | | `estimator` | Estimator | sonnet / medium | Produces per-task time estimates, identifies parallelizable tasks, and lists blocking dependencies. | | `challenger` | Challenger | sonnet / medium | Reviews missing work, ordering, prescription, batching, error handling, criterion coverage, and shared-interface siblings. Interface coverage uses live syntax and architecture evidence, not memory alone. Capped at 2 review rounds. | --- ## Pipeline ```mermaid %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'flowchart': {'curve': 'basis', 'nodeSpacing': 40, 'rankSpacing': 56}, 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'Inter, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif', 'fontSize': '14px', 'lineColor': '#94a3b8', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#ffffff'}}}%% flowchart LR classDef source fill:#eef2ff,stroke:#6366f1,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#1e1b4b,rx:10px,ry:10px,font-weight:600; classDef store fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#0f172a,rx:10px,ry:10px; classDef engine fill:#f5f3ff,stroke:#8b5cf6,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#4c1d95,rx:10px,ry:10px; classDef router fill:#fffbeb,stroke:#f59e0b,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#78350f,rx:10px,ry:10px,font-weight:600; classDef output fill:#ecfdf5,stroke:#10b981,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#064e3b,rx:10px,ry:10px,font-weight:600; Spec["spec@1"] --> Planner["Planner
subsystem batches"] Planner --> Challenger{{"Challenger
adversarial review"}} Challenger -.->|"targeted findings"| Planner Challenger -->|"pass"| Plan[("plan@1
written + committed")] Plan -.->|"optional"| Estimator["Estimator
effort range"] class Spec source class Planner engine class Challenger router class Plan output class Estimator store ``` `estimator` is optional — run it when scheduling matters. `challenger` always runs; its findings are fed back to `planner` for targeted fixes, capped at 2 rounds before minor disagreements are demoted to non-blocking. --- ## Output Schema `plan@1` — see `shared/schemas/plan@1.json` The plan is an ordered array of tasks. Each task has: `id`, `title`, `files`, `steps`, `commit_message`, `depends_on`, `covers_criteria`. The plan itself carries `spec_file_path` (propagated from the spec), `spec_hash` (a content hash of the spec file at plan time, used by `recon` to detect if the spec changed after planning), `linked_requirement` (propagated from the spec's `linked_requirement`, so the requirement-to-code chain stays traceable without re-reading the spec), and `plan_file_path` --- ## Task Requirements Every task in `plan@1` must include all of the following. Tasks missing any field are rejected: - **Exact file paths** to create or modify (no "create a file for X") - **A brief implementation approach**, decided before the test steps are written - **The outcome** the task leaves true, and the **signatures or interfaces** it adds or changes, with error behavior - **Implementation code only where the logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape would be costly** (concurrency or ordering, numeric or parsing edge cases, security checks, wire or on-disk formats, signatures other tasks depend on); routine code gets the outcome and signature. Any code is a baseline smith's implementer may adapt - **The exact tests** proving each of the task's `covers_criteria` criteria (inputs and asserted results), with the verification command confirming the full suite passes - **A conventional commit message** for the task - **`covers_criteria`** — the acceptance criterion IDs from the spec this task addresses Tests are not required to precede the implementation steps within a task. See [ADR-008](../../docs/adr/008-drop-test-first-ordering.md) and smith's [Implementation Cycle](../smith/README.md#implementation-cycle-per-task) for that rationale, and [ADR-009](../../docs/adr/009-implementer-shape-latitude.md) and [ADR-014](../../docs/adr/014-outcome-level-plans.md) for why plan code is a baseline, and only where it earns its cost. No TBDs. No "the implementer will decide" about scope, files, interfaces, or proof. Every acceptance criterion must appear in at least one task's `covers_criteria` — `challenger` flags any criterion that appears in none as `orphaned-criteria`. --- ## Next Stage Feed `plan@1` to **[smith](../smith/)** (implementation). --- name: plan description: >- Trigger when the user asks to plan, break down, or sequence the implementation of a spec ("write a plan for X", "break this down into tasks", "plan this out"), or when a spec@1 exists and implementation is next. Also covers estimating or challenging an existing plan. Produces a plan@1 of executable tasks linked to acceptance criteria. version: 1.5.0 --- # Navigator Planning Skill Navigator decomposes a spec@1 into a sequenced, bite-sized plan@1 that a developer or agent can execute without deciding what to build, where, or what proves it. Every task states its outcome, files, signatures, and proving tests, and carries implementation code only where the logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape would be costly. Every task is independently testable. --- navigator is one skill, `plan`. Behavior adapts to what's asked, dispatching to whichever agent below fits the request — there is no separate `navigator/estimate` or `navigator/challenge` skill to invoke; estimating and challenging both happen inside this one skill. - **Decompose a spec** — `planner` creates ordered, subsystem-batched tasks. - Read and propagate persisted spec metadata. - In amend mode, change only tasks tied to corrected criteria. - **Estimate an existing plan** — `estimator` assigns effort estimates (in minutes) to each task in a plan@1, identifies parallelizable tasks, and surfaces blocking dependencies. - **Challenge a draft plan** — `challenger` checks coverage, order, specificity (outcome, signatures, tests, command; no full bodies for routine code), batch size, error handling, and shared-interface siblings. It loads `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/references/verification/interface-coverage.md` when a contract or implementation changes. Amended plans receive the same review. --- | Agent | Role | Model / Effort | Delegate When | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **planner** | Plan author | sonnet / medium | Decompose a spec into ordered, subsystem-batched implementation tasks. | | **estimator** | Effort estimator | sonnet / medium | Assign time estimates, identify parallelizable tasks, and surface blocking dependencies. | | **challenger** | Adversarial reviewer | sonnet / medium | Stress-test a draft plan@1 before any implementation begins. Two rounds at most; if it still fails, stop and put the remaining issues to the user. | --- **Consumes**: `spec@1` (or its `spec_file_path`, read from disk when set) **Produces**: `plan@1` — carries `spec_file_path`, `spec_hash`, and `linked_requirement` propagated from the source spec --- After `challenger` returns an overall `pass` verdict, THE SKILL SHALL, before handing off to `smith`: 1. Write the plan@1 JSON to `/docs/projects/.json`. Create the directory if it does not exist. 2. Commit the file to version control. An uncommitted plan file is invisible to a fresh checkout and a future session, the same way an uncommitted spec is invisible to `scribe/spec-drift`. 3. Set `plan_file_path` to the workspace-relative path (e.g. `docs/projects/SPEC-001.json`) in the plan@1 object. 4. Pass the updated plan@1 — with `plan_file_path` set — to `smith`. An amended plan (planner's amend mode, following a spec correction) overwrites the file at the same `plan_file_path` and commits the change — the path does not change across an amendment, mirroring `scribe/correct-spec`'s rule for corrected specs. The amended plan still passes through `challenger` before this write, per the Spec Correction Loop. Without `plan_file_path` set, `weaver/audit-backlog` and other downstream agents fall back to treating plan coverage as unverifiable for that requirement, the same graceful-degradation posture as an unset `spec_file_path`. --- Test steps are not required to precede implementation steps within a task. Smith's mutation-testing gate — not step order — is what verifies a test would actually catch a wrong implementation; a controlled comparison found no quality advantage from write-test-first ordering for agent-written code, at several times the token cost, and found it suppressed upfront design work agents otherwise did well ([Böckeler, "TDD inside the agent loop"](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/tdd-in-the-agent-loop.html)). A task with no test proving a covers_criteria criterion violates this requirement — the criterion has no evidence, regardless of write order. Plan code is optional and, where present, a baseline; see [ADR-009](../../../../docs/adr/009-implementer-shape-latitude.md) for the implementer's latitude and [ADR-014](../../../../docs/adr/014-outcome-level-plans.md) for when a plan carries code.

Smith never assembles a changeset itself. It hands `criteria_evidence` — exact test and implementation locations for every criterion it proved — to **[courier](../courier/)**, which produces `changeset@2` from it. --- ## When to Use - You have a `plan@1` and want it executed task-by-task - You have a `spec@1` but no plan, and want to implement directly - You need proof — not just a claim — that every acceptance criterion was actually tested, with tests validated by mutation testing rather than a write-first ritual - You want to find out whether a tool, library or approach works before committing to it (`spike`): a throwaway experiment with no plan, spec, review or gate **Invoke with:** `"Implement this"`, `"Execute the plan"`, `"Build this feature"`, `"Spike whether this library works in our stack"` --- ## Install **Claude Code** — add the marketplace once, then install by ID: ``` /plugin marketplace add orin-dx/wisp-plugins /plugin install smith ``` **AGY** — installs the full repo; see the [root README](../../README.md#install) for instructions. **Codex** — see the [root Codex setup](../../README.md#codex), then run `codex plugin add smith@wisp-plugins`. --- ## Skills | Skill | What it does | Subagent | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `smith/implement` | Executes plan batches with risk-matched verification, defect-family review and an independent exit gate | `recon`, `implementer`, `mutator`, `reviewer`, `exit-gate` | | `smith/spike` | Runs the smallest throwaway experiment that answers one question and returns a `spike-report@1` of what was observed, verified and left unchecked. Non-binding: no plan, spec, mutation, review or exit gate | none | Agents are internal to `implement`; invoke the skill, not its agents. `spike` is the light path for early technical questions (see `shared/references/architecture/modes.md`); anything it finds is promoted through `muse/promote`, never treated as evidence for a gate. --- ## Subagents | Subagent | Role | Tier | What it does | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `recon` | Workspace Recon | haiku / low | Detects language, test runner, build tool. Inventories plan files. Confirms the baseline passes before any code is written. Flags `spec_drift_warning` if the plan's `spec_hash` no longer matches the spec file on disk. | | `implementer` | Implementation Executor | sonnet / medium | Designs, implements, and tests one task. Commits only with explicit authorization. Reports contradictions and architecture needs instead of forcing a pass. | | `mutator` | Mutation Gate | sonnet / medium | Runs mutation testing on the task's changed files. Designs a precision test for every surviving mutant. | | `reviewer` | Pre-Gate Review | sonnet / medium | Produces `implementation-review@2`: issues, sibling candidate sites, verification gaps, defect families, and structural assessments. | | `exit-gate` | Adversarial Verifier | opus / high | Independently verifies current code, relevant boundaries, sibling candidates, and completed checks. plan@1 or direct spec@1"] --> Recon["Recon
baseline + capabilities"] subgraph loop ["Per subsystem batch · × N"] direction LR Impl["Implementer

Records one batch outcome, criterion evidence, commands, changed files, gaps, and any spec or architecture escalation. `mutation-report@2` — see `shared/schemas/mutation-report@2.json`. Records the selected method, commands, cases, survivors, generated-input evidence, precision tests, gaps, and errors. `spike-report@1` — see `shared/schemas/spike-report@1.json`. Produced by `spike`: the question, the approach, what was observed, what was verified and what was not, and a conclusion (`works`, `partly`, `fails`, `inconclusive`; `works` needs at least one verified item). Marked `fidelity: spike`; non-binding. The reviewer loads `shared/references/verification/implementation-review.md`, which selects the language hazards, architecture smells, and comment standard relevant to the diff. Each `implementer` batch also returns `criteria_evidence` — one `{criterion_id, test_file, test_line, implementation_file, implementation_line}` entry per criterion the batch proves. A controlled comparison found agent-written code produced no measurable quality advantage from write-test-first ordering, at 3–9x the token cost, and that forcing a failing test into existence before any design work suppressed the upfront design agents otherwise did well ([Böckeler, "TDD inside the agent loop"](https://martinfowler.com/arti --- ## Mutation Gate (per subsystem batch) After implementation, `mutator` uses the project-native mutation tool when available. Otherwise it performs a safe deliberate-fault check or records the missing capability. Property, fuzz, race, integration, and boundary checks are selected when they fit the changed risk; generative checks must name their generator and oracle. For every surviving mutant, it designs a precision test that would kill it and returns those to `implementer` to write and make pass. Only when zero mutants survive — or the tool is unavailable, recorded as a gap rather than a block — does the batch move to `reviewer`. --- ## Defect-Family Review Reviewer searches for the same syntax or algorithm and for different code expressing the same domain responsibility or failure state. Related instances are grouped by root cause and assessed for missing concepts, states, operations, boundaries, abstractions, invariants, or enforcement. - Scoped instances return to `implementer` for repair. - Duplicated logic is unified when one implementation can own the behavior. - Structural gaps route to `scribe:architect` before work resumes. - Deferrals require an explicit reason for every affected instance. --- ## Exit Gate `exit-gate` runs after all batches have approved reviews. It reads current code independently, validates `implementation-review@2`, derives its own sibling candidates, and verifies each structural disposition and relevant boundary before returning `verdict@3`. On fail, blockers go back to `implementer` for a targeted fix — one retry, then escalate to a human if the second round fails or a blocker repeats. --- ## Next Stage Feed `verdict@3` to **[sentinel](../sentinel/)** for standalone gate verification. Hand the accumulated `criteria_evidence` to **[courier](../courier/)** for commit, PR, changeset, and release tooling.

---
name: implement
description: >-
  Activate for implementation, implementation tests, or behavior-preserving refactoring from a plan@1, spec@1, or fix brief. Runs bounded batches with recon, mutation, defect-family review, and an exit gate, returning implementation-result@1 and a scoped verdict@3. Not for explanation-only requests.
version: 1.7.0
---

# Smith — Implementation Skill

<capability>
Smith executes cohesive subsystem batches. Workspace discovery records languages and available capabilities; implementation selects evidence from changed risks; review checks verification and defect families; the exit gate limits its verdict to observed scope.
</capability>

<io>
**Consumes**: `plan@1`, `spec@1` when no plan exists, or a fix brief for findings and diff-sized changes (see `fix_pass`); optionally `implementation-context@1` from Wisp.

**Produces**: committed code when authorized, `workspace-manifest@1`, `implementation-result@1`, `mutation-report@2`, `implementation-review@2`, and `verdict@3`.

The caller aggregates `criteria_evidence` for exit-gate and later passes it with the diff to `courier:changeset`.
</io>

# guide — Start Here

**Stage:** Any · **Output:** routes to the right skill · **Version:** 1.0.0

Six commands named by what you want, not by which plugin does it. Each says which mode it chose and hands off to the skill that does the work, so that skill's checks run.

---

## When to Use

- You want options before deciding: `/guide:explore`
- You want to know whether something works: `/guide:spike`
- Something is broken, or a review left findings: `/guide:fix`
- You are building something real: `/guide:build`
- You want work verified or bugs found: `/guide:check`
- The work is ready to commit, document or release: `/guide:ship`

---

## Skills

| Skill | Does | Hands off to |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `guide/explore` | Structurally different options, rendered, with a decision log | `muse:sketch`, then `muse:promote` |
| `guide/spike` | The smallest throwaway experiment that answers one question | `smith:spike` |
| `guide/fix` | A fix with a test that fails on the original bug, a review and an exit check | `smith:implement` (fix path) |
| `guide/build` | A path chosen by risk: gated spec and plan for shared work, a brief for contained work | `scribe`/`muse`, `navigator:plan`, `smith:implement` |
| `guide/check` | Verification against criteria, or a defect hunt | `sentinel:gate`, `ranger:audit` |
| `guide/ship` | Commit message, changeset, pull request, release notes | `courier` skills |

The pipeline plugins also refuse a direct call to one of their agents once per session until one of their skills has started, and say which skill to use. A second direct call goes through, so a deliberate direct use still works.

---

## Add to your project's AGENTS.md

```markdown
## Plugins
Start work through these commands so their checks run:
- options before deciding: /guide:explore — does it work: /guide:spike
- bug or review findings: /guide:fix — real feature or shared change: /guide:build
- verify or find bugs: /guide:check — commit, changeset, PR, release: /guide:ship
```

---

## Install

**Claude Code** — add the marketplace once, then install by ID:
```
/plugin marketplace add orin-dx/wisp-plugins
/plugin install guide
```

The commands hand off to skills in `muse`, `smith`, `scribe`, `navigator`, `sentinel`, `ranger` and `courier`; install the ones you use.

1 # Contributing
   2 
   3 By participating in this project, you agree to abide by the [Code of Conduct](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Found a security issue? See [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md) instead of opening a public issue.
   4 
   5 ---
   6 
   7 ## Authoring a New Plugin
   8 
   9 The fastest way to scaffold a new plugin is with the `mason` plugin:
  10 
  11 ```
  12 "Create a plugin called <id> that does <goal>"
  13 ```
  14 
  15 `scaffolder` generates the full directory structure, `plugin.json`, `SKILL.md`, and stub subagent files. Run `auditor` afterward to verify conformance.
  16 
  17 To scaffold manually:
  18 
  19 ```bash
  20 mkdir -p plugins/<id>/skills/<id> plugins/<id>/agents
  21 ln -s ../../shared plugins/<id>/shared
  22 ```
  23 
  24 Then create `plugin.json`, `skills/<id>/SKILL.md`, and `agents/*.md` following the conventions below.
  25 
  26 ---
  27 
  28 ## Plugin Structure
  29 
  30 ```
  31 plugins/<id>/
  32 ├── plugin.json
  33 ├── README.md
  34 ├── CHANGELOG.md
  35 ├── skills/<id>/SKILL.md
  36 └── agents/
  37     ├── scanner.md       (sonnet/medium — pattern matching)
  38     ├── worker.md        (sonnet/medium — analysis)
  39     ├── adversary.md     (opus/high — adversarial reasoning)
  40     └── exit-gate.md     (opus/high — final judgment)
  41 ```
  42 
  43 Organize agents by **cognitive mode**, not pipeline position. A scan agent and an analysis agent require different mental modes — split them even if they run sequentially. Agent files are never prefixed with the plugin id (`worker.md`, not `my-plugin-worker.md`) — Claude Code already namespaces agents as `<plugin_id>:<agent_name>`, so a prefix produces redundant `my-plugin
  44 
  45 A plugin defaults to this single-skill layout. IF its scope covers several genuinely independent, heterogeneous intents on the same artifact — not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow — `skills/<id>/` may split into `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill instead (see `courier`, `scribe`, `weaver`, `mason`). A new skill name defaults to a single lifecycle-stage word; go 
  46 
  47 ### `plugin.json`
  48 
  49 ```json
  50 {
  51   "id": "my-plugin",
  52   "name": "my-plugin",
  53   "version": "1.0.0",
  54   "description": "One sentence.",
  55   "author": {

# Cross-Harness Authoring

Use this guide when a change affects Claude/AGY source plugins, Codex-native plugins, shared artifact contracts, or generated Codex distribution.

## Design boundary

Shared sources preserve lifecycle identity and interoperable artifacts. Harness sources preserve execution quality. Never mechanically translate prompts, model tiers, named agents, or delegation topology across harnesses.

| Concern | Shared source | Claude/AGY source | Codex source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Identity | ID, version, author, `consumes`, `produces` | Uses `plugins/<id>/plugin.json` | Native manifest matches ID, version, and author |
| Artifact contract | Versioned JSON schema | Produces and consumes the schema | Produces and consumes the same schema bytes |
| Skill inventory | Lifecycle route name | `plugins/<id>/skills/<skill>/` | Same route name under `harnesses/codex/plugins/<id>/skills/` |
| Workflow | None | Specialist agents and Claude-native orchestration | Native skill plus optional Codex role cards |
| Delegation | None | Named source agents | `agent-roles/<role>.md` selected only for bounded independent work |

## 11. Just-In-Time (JIT) Context Hooks & Tool Guidance

To prevent context bloat, deliver tool preferences and language taxonomies dynamically via lifecycle hooks. `shared/hooks/` holds `validate-handback.py`, which the five gate plugins register through `hooks/hooks.json` (ADR 012), and two reference scripts that no plugin wires:

- **`PreToolUse` shell hook:** injects a short modern CLI hint on first shell use.
- **`SubagentStart` language hook:** detects manifests and binds the language hazard taxonomy.
- **AST search:** keep discovery interfaces replaceable by dedicated symbol tools such as `monokl`.

---

## How It Works

Sentinel is a single skill (`sentinel:sentinel` — the frontmatter `name: gate` is a cosmetic label, not the routing key; skills route by directory name) — not a set of per-artifact-type sub-skills. The same three-agent chain runs unchanged no matter what you hand it; `recon` is what determines the artifact type and derives its criteria, so nothing about the pipeline itself needs to vary by type.

# muse — Component Specification

**Stage:** Design · **Output:** `spec@1` · **Version:** 1.2.0

Turns UI or design intent into a component spec a developer can implement — including its accessibility behavior — without a single clarifying question. Muse audits the spec, not the implementation. It also has a light, non-binding path for early work: see options first, decide, then carry the choice forward.

- **Drafts** a component spec from a requirement or free-text design intent: props, variants, every interactive state, and accessibility criteria as testable propositions
- **Audits** the draft for missing states, missing accessibility criteria, and unmarked invalid prop combinations
- **Gates** the spec with a binding, default-fail exit gate before it proceeds to planning
- **Sketches** structurally different options, rendered and shown before they are described, with a decision log — no gate, no spec, no tests
- **Promotes** a chosen option into a `requirement@1`, the only route from a sketch into the gated stages

The `component` skill is one draft-audit-gate pipeline, reused unchanged regardless of which component is being specified. `sketch` and `promote` are the exploration path and never gate anything (see `shared/references/architecture/modes.md`).

---

## When to Use

- You have a `requirement@1` (or a design description/mockup) and need a formal component spec
- You want to check a drafted component spec for missing interactive states or ARIA criteria before it's implemented
- You need a binding pass/fail gate on a component spec before it enters planning
- You are about to write a component spec by hand: invoke `muse/component` first
- You want to see a few directions for a screen or component before deciding what to build (`sketch`), or a chosen option is ready to become real work (`promote`)

**Invoke with:** `"Spec this component"`, `"Draft a component spec for this design"`, `"Audit this component spec"`, `"Is this component spec ready?"`, `"Gate this component spec"`, `"Show me some options for this screen"`, `"Promote option B"`

Muse specs the component, not the code that implements it. Code-level accessibility scanning of the built component is not yet covered: **[ranger](../ranger/)** has no accessibility hazard pack.

---

## Install

**Claude Code** — add the marketplace once, then install by ID:
```
/plugin marketplace add orin-dx/wisp-plugins
/plugin install muse
```

**AGY** — installs the full repo; see the [root README](../../README.md#install) for instructions.

**Codex** — see the [root Codex setup](../../README.md#codex), then run `codex plugin add muse@wisp-plugins`.

---

## Skills

| Skill | What it does | Subagent |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `muse/component` | Drafts, audits, and gates a component `spec@1` — props, variants, per-state behavior, and accessibility criteria as testable propositions | `drafter`, `auditor`, `exit-gate` |
| `muse/sketch` | Builds and renders three structurally different options per round, shows them before describing them, and keeps a decision log in an `option-set@1`. Non-binding: no gate, no spec, no tests | `explorer` |
| `muse/promote` | Turns a chosen option (or a spike that worked) into a `requirement@1` that carries the decision, the approved render, and what was and was not verified | none |

`component` is one skill, not three — the request itself determines which stage runs; there is no separate `muse/draft` or `muse/audit` to invoke.

---

## Subagents

| Subagent | Role | Tier | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |

**`spec@1`** — see `shared/schemas/spec@1.json` (same schema `scribe` produces; muse introduces no new shape)

| Field | Required | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `id` | yes | Unique spec identifier |
| `purpose` | yes | One-sentence statement of what this component accomplishes |
| `scope` | yes | What is in scope for this spec |
| `non_goals` | yes | Explicit list of what this spec does NOT cover — including any state deliberately left unspecified |
| `api_surface` | no | The component's props — one entry per prop, `signature` carrying its type/domain |
| `acceptance_criteria` | yes | Array of testable propositions covering every prop, variant, state, and accessibility criterion; each has `is_error_case` flag |
| `spec_file_path` | no | Workspace-relative path where this spec is written on disk. Set after `exit-gate` passes. |
| `revision_note` | no | Set only on a correction — what changed and why, citing the affected criterion_id |
| `reasoning` | yes | Scratchpad — never forwarded downstream |

# muse — Component Specification

**Stage:** Design · **Output:** `spec@1` · **Version:** 1.2.0

Turns UI or design intent into a component spec a developer can implement — including its accessibility behavior — without a single clarifying question. Muse audits the spec, not the implementation. It also has a light, non-binding path for early work: see options first, decide, then carry the choice forward.

- **Drafts** a component spec from a requirement or free-text design intent: props, variants, every interactive state, and accessibility criteria as testable propositions
- **Audits** the draft for missing states, missing accessibility criteria, and unmarked invalid prop combinations
- **Gates** the spec with a binding, default-fail exit gate before it proceeds to planning
- **Sketches** structurally different options, rendered and shown before they are described, with a decision log — no gate, no spec, no tests
- **Promotes** a chosen option into a `requirement@1`, the only route from a sketch into the gated stages

The `component` skill is one draft-audit-gate pipeline, reused unchanged regardless of which component is being specified. `sketch` and `promote` are the exploration path and never gate anything (see `shared/references/architecture/modes.md`).

---

## When to Use

- You have a `requirement@1` (or a design description/mockup) and need a formal component spec
- You want to check a drafted component spec for missing interactive states or ARIA criteria before it's implemented
- You need a binding pass/fail gate on a component spec before it enters planning
- You are about to write a component spec by hand: invoke `muse/component` first
- You want to see a few directions for a screen or component before deciding what to build (`sketch`), or a chosen option is ready to become real work (`promote`)

**Invoke with:** `"Spec this component"`, `"Draft a component spec for this design"`, `"Audit this component spec"`, `"Is this component spec ready?"`, `"Gate this component spec"`, `"Show me some options for this screen"`, `"Promote option B"`

Muse specs the component, not the code that implements it. Code-level accessibility scanning of the built component is not yet covered: **[ranger](../ranger/)** has no accessibility hazard pack.

---

**Claude Code** — add the marketplace once, then install by ID:

ranger: Bug hunting for Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, and Go. Confirms reachable defects, searches semantic siblings, and routes structural families for architectural correction.
sentinel: Cross-cutting verification gate. Confirms that any stage artifact meets its criteria before the next stage begins. One skill, one recon-verify-judge pipeline, reused unchanged against any artifact type.
weaver: Need definition plugin. Captures and structures requirements before implementation begins. Integrates with GitHub Issues by default; extensible to Linear, Jira, or any issue tracker that produces the requirement@1 schema. Skills: capture-need, clarify-requirement, prioritize-backlog, connect-requirement, audit-backlog.
vanguard: Research plugin. Investigates questions and requirements to build a documented evidence base before committing to a solution direction. Produces research-report@1 for consumption by scribe (spec).
scribe: Specification plugin. Turns requirements and research reports into unambiguous, testable specs. Checks specs against a persisted whole-system architecture model. Detects spec drift against actual code. Skills: draft-spec, verify-spec, spec-drift, audit-spec, audit-architecture, gate-spec, correct-spec, architect.
muse: Component specification plugin. Turns UI/design intent into unambiguous, testable component specs — props, variants, per-state behavior, and accessibility criteria as testable propositions, gated before planning. Audits the spec, not the implementation; code-level accessibility scanning of the built component is not yet covered by ranger. Also sketches options before anything is specified (sketch) and carries a chosen option into a requirement (promote).
navigator: Planning plugin. Decomposes specs into sequenced, bite-sized implementation plans with an implementation approach, exact code as a baseline, and the tests proving each criterion — no write-test-first mandate. Tasks are sized to compilation boundaries, not a clock-time estimate. No TBDs. A developer with zero domain context can execute the plan mechanically.
smith: Implementation plugin. Executes tested plan batches, verifies risk at real boundaries, searches semantic defect siblings, and escalates shared model or architecture gaps. Also spikes: a throwaway experiment that checks whether a tool or approach works (spike).
courier: Shipping plugin. Shepherds completed code through commit, PR creation, review response, and changeset documentation. Skills: commit, pr, changeset, receive-feedback, post-review, release.

# Changelog

All notable changes to the Wisp Plugins ecosystem are documented here.
Individual plugin changelogs live in `plugins/<plugin-id>/CHANGELOG.md`.

## [4.6.0] - 2026-11-14 — Start by intent, two rounds, one reality check

- New `guide` plugin: `/guide:explore`, `spike`, `fix`, `build`, `check` and `ship` start work by intent and hand off to the skill that does it, with a snippet for a project's `AGENTS.md`.
- The six pipeline plugins redirect a direct call to one of their agents, once per session, to the skill that starts it, so its checks run.
- Exit gates and the plan challenger get two rounds; after a second failing round, or a repeated blocker, the decision goes to a human (ADR 015, amends ADR 012's cap of three).
- Spec drafters self-check and the gate judges; auditor, verifier and architecture audit run on request or for shared or cross-module specs. Spec gates check claims against the code, build or spec they cite.
- Implementation review runs once per batch; mutation is skipped when a batch changes no executable logic.
- Gates, reviewers and verifiers count only behavior run with real inputs as evidence that logic works; visual changes are checked in the built page where a browser exists.
- Pipeline agents' descriptions name the skill that starts them, so the skill's checks run; resident description text is about 27% smaller.

## [4.5.0] - 2026-11-10 — Exploration modes, enforced gates, layered changesets

- Added exploration modes: `muse/sketch`, `muse/promote`, `smith/spike` and the `explorer` agent, with `option-set@1` and `spike-report@1` (ADR 011). Exploration never gates and enters the pipeline only through `promote`.
- Gate output is checked by a hook in the five gate plugins, including the retry cap (ADR 012). Exit gates list the complete blocker set in round one and drafters self-check (ADR 013).
- Plans state outcomes and contracts and carry code only where it earns its cost (ADR 014, partially supersedes ADR 009).
- Courier writes layered changesets without a length cap: `changeset@3` and `release-artifact@3`; `commit-analyzer` and `pr-narrator` follow the repository's own conventions.
- The `muse` gate returns `verdict@3`; a light `smith` entry handles review findings; a hazard reference covers scripts, CI workflows and templates.
- Agent and skill descriptions are about half the size, skills lead with the request they serve, and shared references load from the plugin root so agents find them on the first read.
- The two `claude-fable-5-1` agents (`scribe:arch-auditor`, `scribe:architect`) and the Codex `judge` role (`gpt-6-astra`) move one tier down (`opus / high`, `gpt-6.1-sol / high`) for cost; no heavier tier is defined. The Codex `author` role uses `gpt-6.1-terra / medium`.
- Marketplace sources are relative paths, so installed plugins include their shared schemas and references.

## [4.4.5] - 2026-09-27 — Architecture model decision links

- Added `arch-model@2`: invariants may cite a `decision_ref` naming the governing decision record. `arch-model@1` unchanged; an existing persisted model needs no migration.
- Trimmed all 10 plugin CHANGELOGs for scannability — no behavior change.

## [4.4.4] - 2026-09-27 — Language-service evidence

- Restored Smith's language-service evidence guidance (LSP diagnostics count as supporting boundary evidence only with recorded backend identity/version and capability match), lost during the prior release and recovered from session history.

## [4.4.3] - 2026-09-27 — Decision records and AGENTS.md consolidation

- Added a decision-record convention (`shared/references/architecture/decision-records.md`) and a `docs/adr/` index with a guardrail per record, checked by a new reference-integrity test.
- Removed `CLAUDE.md`; `AGENTS.md` is now the sole source of truth for every harness.
- Ranger's adversary sweep follows `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md`'s `@` imports and the nearest nested instruction file.

# Evaluation runbook

How to run the paired design in `docs/evaluation-methodology.md` on real work, for three task kinds. The question each time: does the treatment reduce turns and tokens, and does the first result need less rework? Single-run pilots and anecdotes cannot answer that. Pairs can, within the limits below.

`tools/transcript-metrics.py turns`, `agents`, `context` and `gates` measure; `tools/paired-analysis.py compare` and `agreement` analyse. `tests/test_transcript_metrics.py` (`DryRunTests`) runs this pipeline on synthetic sessions.

## Before any run

1. **Write the task list and the checklists first.** Take 6 to 10 real tasks from the backlog, each with a blinded checklist (see Scoring). Nothing is edited after the first run.
2. **Pin everything but the treatment.** Same model id, effort, repo commit, permission mode, and CLAUDE.md and memory. Record plugin versions and dates (methodology rule 10). Start each run in a fresh session from a clean checkout of the repo state.
3. **Randomize order.** Flip a coin per task for which arm runs first, so fatigue and your own learning do not fall on one arm. Run each pair on the same day.
4. **Run each arm per task once, then repeat** when you can: two to three runs, reduced to the median per task.
5. **One person drives, another scores.** The driver answers the agent's questions the same way in both arms (write the answers down on the first run and reuse them). Stop when the driver would accept the result; that is "acceptance".

## Capturing a session

The transcript is `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-project-dir>/<session-id>.jsonl` (read only; never copy it into the repo). For each finished run:

```
python3 tools/transcript-metrics.py turns --file <transcript> --trial task=T1,arm=control,run=1,score=0.7,defects=2 >> trials.jsonl
python3 tools/transcript-metrics.py context --match '<project-dir-suffix>$'
python3 tools/transcript-metrics.py agents --match '<project-dir-suffix>$'
python3 tools/transcript-metrics.py gates <directory holding <spec>-verdict[-n].json>
```

Add `gate_rounds=N` to `--trial` for the spec task and `ctx_chars=N` from `context`'s total. The `turns` fields: `prompts` (human prompts, the turns to acceptance), `turns` (assistant messages), `tool_calls`, `subagents`, `retries` (a call right after a failure, same tool, changed input; rework signal, defined in the tool docstr

Then:

```
python3 tools/paired-analysis.py compare trials.jsonl --baseline control --metrics score,prompts,turns,retries,subagent_tokens,gate_rounds
```

## Task kinds

### A. Design ideation (muse or sketch against an ad hoc session)

- **Statement**: "Explore <N=3> directions for <screen or component> in <repo>. Constraints: <list>. Stop when I can pick one."
- **Control**: plain session, no plugin, the same statement. **Treatment**: `muse:sketch` with the plugin installed.
- **Fixed**: model, effort, repo commit, design tokens and brief, the driver's selection rule (pick the option meeting the constraints; ties go to the first).
- **Primary metrics**: prompts to acceptance, `subagent_tokens`, `context` characters by origin, quality score, and whether the chosen direction survives promotion to a spec without being redone.
- **Defects found later**: constraint violations a reviewer finds in the accepted option within one week.

### B. Spec drafting and gating (gated pipeline now versus before gate hygiene)

- **Statement**: "Draft and gate a spec for <requirement>" with a requirement of fixed text.
- **Control**: the plugins at commit `50bdcf1b^` (before the gate-hygiene change), checked out in a separate worktree and loaded as the plugin source. **Treatment**: the plugins at the commit under test. Disable the installed marketplace copy in both so only one version loads, and record the commit in each trial.
- **Fixed**: requirement text, model, effort, a prewritten set of answers to clarifying questions, retry cap.
- **Primary metrics**: `gate_rounds` (from `gates`), blockers per round, `subagent_tokens` from `agents`, prompts to a passed gate, long summaries and escalations.
- **Defects found later**: criteria that a reviewer who has not seen the gate verdicts finds untestable, missing an error case or contradicting the requirement; and spec contradictions raised when the spec is implemented.

### C. Changeset and PR text (courier with layered `changeset@3` guidance versus freehand)

- **Statement**: "Write the changeset and PR description for this diff" with a stored diff (`gh pr diff <n>` saved outside the repo, or a branch to check out).
- **Control**: freehand, no courier skills, no changeset guidance in context. **Treatment**: `courier:changeset` then `courier:pr`.
- **Fixed**: diff, repo conventions file and PR template, model, effort.
- **Primary metrics**: prompts to acceptance, `retries`, tokens (`agents` plus main-thread `context`), characters of text produced, quality score.
- **Defects found later**: a release reader's questions the text did not answer, wrong semver impact, missing limits or breaking-change marks, found by someone who did not write either text.

## Scoring

A scorer who did not run the sessions scores both outputs **blind**: strip arm names, plugin names and agent-specific markers, and shuffle. The checklist is written before the first run and frozen. Each item is yes, no or not applicable, with a one-line evidence note. Score = yes / (yes + no).

```
Task: ___  Output id (shuffled): ___  Scorer: ___  Date: ___
| # | Checklist item (observable, yes or no)        | Yes/No/NA | Evidence |
| 1 | <task-specific, written before the run>        |           |          |
Defects found in later review (count, with one line each): ___
Score: ___ / ___ = ___     Would accept as-is? yes / no
```

Calibration: for task kind B and C, have a second scorer (or an LLM judge) score at least 20 items, then run `python3 tools/paired-analysis.py agreement labels.json` with `[{"a": ..., "b": ...}]`. Use an LLM judge only at kappa of about 0.6 or above (convention, not measured). Below that, score by hand.

## How many pairs, and what a null shows

- The exact Wilcoxon test cannot reach p < 0.05 with fewer than 6 non-tied pairs, whatever the effect. Run **at least 6 pairs per task kind**; aim for 10, with repeats.
- With 6 to 10 pairs only large effects (on the order of a third of turns or tokens, or most items flipping in the checklist) can reach significance. A smaller real effect will look like noise.
- **A null result shows**: no large effect on that task kind, for that model and effort, on those tasks. **It does not show**: no effect, no effect at other efforts, or no effect on other repositories. Report the pair count, the median relative change with its direction, and the better, worse and tied counts. A consistent direct
- Do not mix kinds. Do not drop a task because the treatment lost. A crashed task is dropped from every arm and counted.
- Tag the write-up with `small-sample` and `self-benchmark` where they apply (`docs/evidence-quality.md`).

## Results table

```
| Task kind | Pairs | Prompts (median delta) | Turns | Retries | Subagent tokens | Gate rounds | Score (better/worse/tied) | Defects later | Verdict |
| A ideation |  |  |  |  |  | n/a |  |  |  |
| B spec gate |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| C changeset/PR |  |  |  |  | n/a |  |  |  |
Provenance: model ___, effort ___, plugin commits ___ / ___, repo commit ___, dates ___, runs per task ___, excluded ___.
Power note and what would change the conclusion: ___
```

## Limits

Turn counts depend on how the driver answers. Subagent tokens are reported, not billed, and the main thread's tokens are not in them; `context` counts characters, not tokens, and ignores caching. Retries include legitimate progress. Treat the numbers as a comparison between arms on the same driver, not as absolute costs.

# Codex Marketplace Release Policy

`.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` is the generated Codex discovery manifest at the repository root. It points at the generated `dist/codex` bundle. The authored sources are `plugins/*/plugin.json`, `harnesses/codex/plugins/*/`, `shared/schemas/`, and `harnesses/codex/catalog.json`. Never edit gener

## What is portable

Versioned JSON artifacts in `shared/schemas/` are the compatibility boundary between Claude and Codex. Lifecycle and structural-escalation artifacts move between harnesses by schema ID and JSON content. Named Claude agents, prompt wording, tool availability, and team delegation are not portable cont

The focused compatibility fixture at `tests/fixtures/cross-harness/lifecycle.json` covers the core handoff:

```text
weaver/capture-need  requirement@1  vanguard/research
vanguard/research    research-report@1  scribe/draft-spec
scribe/draft-spec    spec@1  navigator/plan
navigator/plan       plan@1  smith/implement
smith/implement       implementation-review@2  scribe/architect
```

Its test validates fixture documents against the source schemas, confirms the same schema bytes are materialized into the relevant Codex plugins, and checks that both harnesses declare each producer/consumer relationship. It is a contract compatibility evaluation, not proof that two models reach ide

## Change and release procedure

1. Change Claude source manifests, native Codex source files, shared schemas, or the Codex catalog as needed. If a schema changes incompatibly, add a new version; do not modify an existing version.
2. Regenerate the release payload:

   ```bash
   python3 tools/build-codex-marketplace.py
   ```

3. Run the release gates:

   ```bash
   python3 -m unittest tests/test_build_codex_marketplace.py -v
   python3 -m unittest tests/test_cross_harness_artifacts.py -v
   python3 -m unittest tests/test_codex_native_sources.py -v
   python3 tools/build-codex-marketplace.py --check
   ```

4. Review native Codex source and generated changes in the same pull request. A generated change without a native-source, catalog, or schema explanation is a release blocker.
5. Tag and publish only a commit for which the check command succeeds. The tag includes both generated marketplace artifacts so users install a deterministic payload.
6. Register the published bundle with Codex using its marketplace root:

   ```bash
   codex plugin marketplace add orin-dx/wisp-plugins
   ```

   Codex discovers the root manifest and registers this source as `wisp-plugins`; install a plugin with `codex plugin add <plugin>@wisp-plugins`. A source previously registered as `orin-dx-agent-plugins` must be removed and re-added after this release.

CI runs the generator and compatibility tests. A stale generated bundle, a symlink in the bundle, a missing contract, or a mismatch between source and materialized schema must fail before release.

## Behavioral evaluations

The fixture is intentionally narrow. Before declaring a workflow change behaviorally equivalent across harnesses, run a representative task through each harness and compare durable JSON artifacts against the same schema and acceptance criteria. Follow [Cross-Harness Behavioral Evaluation](./codex-be
# ranger — Adversarial Bug Hunting

**Stage:** Cross-cutting · **Output:** `finding-report@2` · **Version:** 3.2.5

Adversarial bug hunting on live Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, and Go code.

- Builds a reachability manifest first, so dead code is never scanned.
- Sweeps live files against language-specific hazard taxonomies, optionally tracing data flow for intent-capture and error-downgrade candidates.
- Refutes every candidate before confirming it — a finding survives only when no refutation can be constructed and a concrete failing scenario can be stated.
- Groups related findings by shared root cause and routes structural families to `scribe:architect`.
- Produces `finding-report@2`, then uses the exit verifier after remediation.

---

## When to Use

- You want a thorough bug hunt across the codebase before a release
- You suspect a specific hazard category (e.g. unsafe memory, unhandled promises) and want a targeted scan
- You have a candidate bug report and want adversarial verification before acting on it
- You want to confirm all findings are resolved after remediation
- You are about to review code for bugs or vulnerabilities by hand: invoke `ranger/audit` first

**Invoke with:** `"Hunt for bugs"`, `"Security audit"`, `"Find vulnerabilities"`, `"Scan for unhandled promises"`, `"Audit this for memory safety issues"`, `"Verify this bug report"`, `"Check what's still broken after my fixes"`

---

## Install

**Claude Code** — add the marketplace once, then install by ID:
```
/plugin marketplace add orin-dx/wisp-plugins
/plugin install ranger
```

**AGY** — installs the full repo; see the [root README](../../README.md#install) for instructions.

**Codex** — see the [root Codex setup](../../README.md#codex), then run `codex plugin add ranger@wisp-plugins`.

---

## How It Works

ranger is one skill, not a menu of sub-commands. The pipeline below is fixed — what changes is which part of the request drives it:

- **Full bug hunt** — no category or candidate named: every hazard taxonomy gets scanned.
- **Targeted scan** — the request names one hazard category (e.g. "unsafe memory", "unhandled promises"): the same pipeline runs, scoped to that category.
- **Verify one candidate** — the request hands ranger an already-identified bug: adversary runs directly against it, skipping the sweep.
- **Post-remediation check** — the request asks whether prior findings are resolved: exit-gate re-reads the code from scratch and confirms.

Unlike `courier` or `scribe`, ranger has exactly one skill directory (`skills/audit/`) — there's no `ranger/scan` or `ranger/verify` to invoke separately.

content.content:
name: Validate

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: 11.9.0

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: pnpm

      - uses: extractions/setup-just@v4

      - name: Install pinned tooling dependencies
        run: just install

      - name: Validate plugin manifests
        run: just manifests

      - name: Run test suite
        run: just test

      - name: Check version consistency
        run: just versions

      - name: Check skill doc accuracy
        run: just skills-doc

      - name: Check reference file size
        run: just reference-size

      - name: Check cross-references and platform description limits
        run: just platform-limits

      - name: Confirm generated Claude plugin manifests are current
        run: just claude-manifests

      - name: Confirm generated Codex marketplace is current
        run: just marketplace-check

      - name: Check Mermaid diagram syntax
        run: just mermaid

      - name: Source wiring
        run: just wiring

      # just fmt-check is not yet in `just check`: the repo isn't formatted
      # with oxfmt yet. Add this step back once that lands.
marketplace-sync:
    python3 tools/build-codex-marketplace.py

# Parse every Mermaid diagram in the repo
mermaid:
    node scripts/check-mermaid.mjs

# Check formatting without writing
fmt-check:
    pnpm exec oxfmt --check .

# Format the repo in place
fmt:
    pnpm exec oxfmt --write .

name: Validate

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with:
          version: 11.9.0

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: pnpm

      - uses: extractions/setup-just@v4

      - name: Install pinned tooling dependencies
        run: just install

      - name: Validate plugin manifests
        run: just manifests

      - name: Run test suite
        run: just test

      - name: Check version consistency
        run: just versions

      - name: Check skill doc accuracy
        run: just skills-doc

      - name: Check reference file size
        run: just reference-size

      - name: Check cross-references and platform description limits
        run: just platform-limits

      - name: Confirm generated Claude plugin manifests are current
        run: just claude-manifests

      - name: Confirm generated Codex marketplace is current
        run: just marketplace-check

      - name: Check Mermaid diagram syntax
        run: just mermaid

      - name: Source wiring
        run: just wiring

      # just fmt-check is not yet in `just check`: the repo isn't formatted
      # with oxfmt yet. Add this step back once that lands.
marketplace-sync:
    python3 tools/build-codex-marketplace.py

# Parse every Mermaid diagram in the repo
mermaid:
    node scripts/check-mermaid.mjs

# Check formatting without writing
fmt-check:
    pnpm exec oxfmt --check .

# Format the repo in place
fmt:
    pnpm exec oxfmt --write .

# Check declared agents, skills and schemas exist for every plugin
wiring:
    bash shared/scripts/validate-wiring.sh

Audit complete: `just check` exits 0, but the docs disagree with the plugins in the places below. Several checks passed. Tiers in plugin READMEs and SKILLs match agent frontmatter, and the agent and skill counts match (45 agents, 11 plugins). `load_first` paths resolve, and every `shared/...` doc path exists except the immutable `changeset@2.json`. I made no edits.

| # | file:line | Inconsistency | Sev. | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ARCHITECTURE.md:127`, `README.md:229`, `docs/pipeline-walkthrough.md:125` | ARCHITECTURE says "no runtime validator runs". README says a schema-invalid output "halts the pipeline". The walkthrough says the synthesizer "couldn't omit the risk finding without schema validation failing". Per `validate-handback.py` and ADR 012, only exit-gate handbacks are checked against `verdict@3`, only in Claude Code auto mode, and the report passes through after 3 denials. | wrong claim | Say that only gate verdicts are hook-validated and that other handoffs are prompt-conformed. |
| 2 | `scribe/skills/{draft-spec:11,26; verify-spec:26; correct-spec:11,34; architect:11; gate-spec:17,29,37; audit-architecture:11,17,33}/SKILL.md` | The skills still prescribe verify → audit-spec → audit-architecture → gate. They describe a "drafter ↔ auditor loop capped at 2" and the gate consuming "post-verify, post-audit-spec". `scribe/README.md:130` and ADR 015 say draft then gate, with the other checks optional. | wrong behavior | Rewrite the routes as "optional, on request, or for shared/cross-module specs". |
| 3 | `ARCHITECTURE.md:203-204`, `plugins/sentinel/README.md:66-67` | Diagram edges say `retry ≤ 3` and `retry > 3`. `ARCHITECTURE.md:217`, `sentinel/README.md:99` and the hook (`RETRY_CAP = 1`) say two rounds. | wrong | Change the edge labels to the two-round rule. |
| 4 | `tools/transcript-metrics.py:199`; `docs/architecture-assumptions.md:15` | `over_retry_cap` counts `retry_count > 3`. Assumption row 7 still reads "retry cap of 3" in its assumption column. | stale | Use `> 1`. Reword the row. |
| 5 | `plugins/sentinel/agents/exit-gate.md:50,52`; `constitution.md:107` | The escalation rule fires at "`retry_count` exceeds 1", and sentinel also says "increment by one". A second failing round has `retry_count` 1, so only a repeated blocker escalates it. ADR 015 says escalate "after the second failing round". `constitution.md:107` also says "a blocker's `retry_count`", but the field is verdict-level. | wrong (ambiguous, medium confidence) | State who increments, and at which round `escalation_required` appears. |
| 6 | `plugins/muse/README.md:81`, `:12`, `:9` | The diagram draws Auditor as a mandatory step before the gate, and the prose says a "draft-audit-gate pipeline". The README's own line 89 and `component/SKILL.md:32` say the auditor runs only when asked. | wrong | Make the auditor an optional dashed edge, as the scribe README does. |
| 7 | `README.md:97,291`; `plugins/courier/README.md:106`; `plugins/smith/README.md:7,120`; `scribe/agents/drift-checker.md:69` (and its description) | Stale schema versions. Root README says `release-artifact@2`, but courier produces `@3`. The courier README says "supersedes `release-artifact@1`", but `@3` supersedes `@2`. The smith README says `changeset@2`, but courier produces `@3`. Drift-checker names `changeset@2`'s `criteria_evidence`. | stale | Change to `@3`, `@2`, `@3`, `@3`. |
| 8 | `docs/pipeline-walkthrough.md:24,47,56,62` | The weaver auditor "checks for testability", but it audits backlog coverage. Scribe's auditor is shown as a default step. Plan tasks carry "exact code" (ADR 014 says outcome-level). Mutation runs "after each task" (it is per batch, skipped when no executable logic). The reviewer and `implementation-review@2` are missing. | stale | Update the four claims. Optionally add the guide entry path. |
| 9 | `marketplace.json` (navigator entry) and `plugins/navigator/plugin.json` description | "exact code as a baseline" and "execute the plan mechanically". `navigator/README.md` and ADR 014 say code only where non-obvious. | stale | Reword the description. This needs a version bump, so a manifest sync. |
| 10 | `plugins/smith/README.md` (Mutation Gate, pipeline) | "Only when zero mutants survive … does the batch move to reviewer", with no skip rule and an unbounded review loop. `implement/SKILL.md` skips mutation when no executable logic changed and allows one repeat review. | stale | Add both rules. |
| 11 | `README.md:84,78,332-342,274/280` | "five bands plus one" but the table has Start, Define, Design, Build, Verify, Ship plus Meta. The badges omit Start. The repository tree omits `guide` and `shared/hooks`. `verdict@3` is listed twice with different "consumed by" text. | cosmetic-stale | Fix the count, add guide, merge the rows. |
| 12 | `README.md:231,267`, `ARCHITECTURE.md:125`, `CONTRIBUTING.md:155` | "Every schema includes `reasoning`", but `candidate@1` and `implementation-context@1` lack it. `architecture-assumptions.md:14` says "29 of 31 schemas" (now 33 of 35). | stale | Say "new schemas", or note the two exceptions. Update the counts. |
| 13 | `AGENTS.md:33`; `agent-best-practices.md:94,99`; `ARCHITECTURE.md:241` | AGENTS layout says `adversary.md` is sonnet/med, but ranger's adversary is opus/high (CONTRIBUTING.md:39 agrees with opus). The best-practices table lists scanner under haiku-style "Enumeration" and verifier under "Judgment", but both are sonnet/medium and the verifier gives evidence only. ARCHITECTURE says adversarial judgment is opus/high, yet `scribe:auditor`, `muse:auditor` and `navigator:challenger` are sonnet/medium. | wrong-ish | Align the tier rules with the actual assignments. |
| 14 | `ARCHITECTURE.md:47`, `AGENTS.md:37`, `CONTRIBUTING.md:45` | The list of plugins with split skills is `courier, scribe, weaver, mason`. Muse, smith and guide also split. | stale | Add them, or say "for example". |
| 15 | `agent-best-practices.md:228`; ARCHITECTURE/AGENTS/CONTRIBUTING | Only `validate-handback.py` is described as wired. `route-guard.py` is registered in six plugins, and no ADR or architecture section covers it. CONTRIBUTING has no step for adding a route-guard `SUGGEST` entry or a `ROUTES` entry. The "name the skill in the agent description" convention from 4.6.0 is not in the authoring checklist. | doc gap | Add a short hooks section and checklist items. |
| 16 | `plugins/sentinel/README.md:49`; `plugins/sentinel/skills/gate/SKILL.md` | The README says `sentinel:sentinel`. The route is `sentinel:gate` (directory `gate`). The SKILL also has an `<axiom_protocol>` tag, a leftover persona name. | wrong / cosmetic | Use `sentinel:gate`. Rename the tag. |
| 17 | `ARCHITECTURE.md:384-395` | The validation table and the "CI runs" sentence omit `platform-limits`, `claude-manifests` and `wiring`, which are in `just check` and CI. | stale | Add the rows. |
| 18 | `plugins/guide/README.md` vs `constitution.md:283` | The constitution requires an agent table, a pipeline diagram and an output-schema section. The guide README has none of these. It also has no Codex or AGY install lines, though the guide exists for Codex. | cosmetic | Add an exemption clause for agent-less plugins, or add the sections. |

**Not flagged:**
- No old persona names appear outside ADR 005/007/008/010 (historical) and the item 16 tag.
- ADR 013 says "40 agents" and "skills do not yet pass" prior blockers. These are historical records, so I left them.
- `verdict@1`/`@2` say "Escalate at 3", which is immutable.

**Not checked:**
- The `harnesses/codex/**` and `dist/**` content.
- Plugin CHANGELOGs.
- `docs/evaluations/**`, per your instruction.
- Mason's auditor and scaffolder against the constitution's rule that they stay in sync.

6	## Context
7	
8	Three independent reads of the evidence (documented evaluations, session token data across five projects, and what reviewers actually caught) agreed on where review earns its cost. First-round, independent checks against code or a build caught real defects: a spec criterion pointing attestation at the wrong commit, an `init` that writes a config the loader rejects, a plan diagnostic that could never fire, padding that computed to zero in the built page. Later rounds were mostly wording churn or agents working around structural tests: one implementation gate ran 14 rounds after calling the code correct in round 3, one plan ran 29 challenge rounds, and one spec ran 13 gate rounds with blockers returning after clean rounds. The auditor and the exit gate reviewed the same draft, so the gate re-found what the auditor found. Reviewers ran per commit with no logic bug caught, and mutation ran on modules with no executable logic.
9	
10	The details are in `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md` (evidence review section). Part of the reviewer catch-rate report was reconstructed from notes, so its exact counts are approximate; the direction is supported by the gate-round records and session data independently.
11	
12	## Decision
13	
14	- **Two rounds.** Every exit gate and the plan challenger get one retry. After the second failing round, or when a blocker repeats unchanged, the gate returns fail with an `escalation_required` blocker and the decision goes to a human with the persistent blockers. For exit gates the hook enforces it: a fail at `retry_count` 1 (the second round) must carry `escalation_required`, and any later report must be an escalated fail (it allowed three retries, per ADR 012). The challenger's output is not `verdict@3`, so its limit is in its prompt only.
15	- **One check per draft, against reality.** Spec drafters self-check and the exit gate judges. The auditor, verifier and architecture audit run when asked, when a spec is shared by other work, or when it crosses a module boundary. Spec gates check every claim, criterion or citation against the code, configuration, build or spec it refers to; an issue that cannot be tied to a source or to a testability defect is a note, not a blocker.
16	- **Scoped watchers.** The implementation reviewer runs once per batch and gets one repeat. Mutation is skipped, and recorded as `unavailable` with a reason, when a batch changes no executable logic.
17	
18	## Options considered
19	
20	- **Keep a cap of three.** Rejected: the useful catches came in rounds one and two; the long loops cost the most and caught the least.
21	- **Remove the independent gate.** Rejected: the first-round independent check produced every documented catch before code existed.
22	- **Cap at one round.** Rejected: one targeted retry fixes most first-round blockers and is cheap.

# Wisp Plugins AI Agent & Skill Specification (`AGENTS.md`)

This guide defines the top-level repository guidelines for AI coding agents (Claude Code, AGY, Cursor, Copilot, Codex) working on or utilizing the Wisp Plugins repository (`orin-dx/wisp-plugins`).

---

## 1. Authoritative Sources

All hard rules for plugin and agent authoring live in one place:

- [**`shared/constitution.md`**](./shared/constitution.md): EARS-format authoritative constraints. The fence all plugin development must stay inside. Read this first and last.
- [**`shared/agent-best-practices.md`**](./shared/agent-best-practices.md): Principles behind the constitution, explained with examples. Authoring-time only — never loaded by agents at runtime.
- [**`shared/debugging-laws.md`**](./shared/debugging-laws.md): Core proof laws, read-only investigation rules, Red-to-Green verification standards.
- [**`shared/harness-authoring.md`**](./shared/harness-authoring.md): Cross-harness change classification, native workflow boundaries, and required counterpart review.
- [**`docs/adr/README.md`**](./docs/adr/README.md): Index of accepted architectural decisions, each with a guardrail. Read the record before changing what its guardrail names; [`shared/references/architecture/decision-records.md`](./shared/references/architecture/decision-records.md) says when and how to write one.
- [**`shared/references/tooling/cli.md`**](./shared/references/tooling/cli.md): Capability-aware preferences for modern CLI tools, with repository-native commands and safe fallbacks taking priority.

---

## 2. Directory Layout Standard

```text
plugins/<plugin-id>/
├── plugin.json                   <-- Plugin Manifest (id, version, skills, agents)
├── README.md                     <-- Purpose, trigger phrases, agent table, install
├── CHANGELOG.md                  <-- Semver history
├── skills/
│   └── <plugin-id>/
│       └── SKILL.md              <-- Skill definition (dispatch matrix, pipeline)
└── agents/
    ├── recon.md                  <-- haiku/low  — deterministic enumeration
    ├── scanner.md                <-- sonnet/med — pattern matching
    ├── adversary.md              <-- sonnet/med — adversarial verification
    └── exit-gate.md              <-- opus/high  — binding judgment
```

A plugin defaults to one skill directory named after the plugin id, as above. IF the plugin's scope covers several genuinely independent, heterogeneous intents on the same artifact — not a linear pipeline invoked as one flow — `skills/<plugin-id>/` may split into `skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` per skill instead. `courier`, `scribe`, `weaver`, and `mason` are examples. The skill-routing key is the directory name, not the frontmatter `name:` field. A new skill name defaults to a single lifecycle-stage word; only go to a specific compound name (`audit-spec`, not `scribe-audit`) when the bare word is ambiguous or collides with another plugin's existing skill name. See `shared/constitution.md`'s Plugin Structure and Skill Names sections.

Agents are organized by **cognitive mode** (enumeration, tracing, adversarial, systemic, behavioral, judgment, repair) — not by pipeline position. See `shared/constitution.md` for the model/effort tier rules.

---

## 3. Quick Checklist for Adding New Plugins

1. **Use `mason`** — run `scaffolder` to generate the full directory structure and stubs.
2. **5-part agent structure** — every agent body: `<constitution>` (copied byte-for-byte from an existing agent), `<backstory>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, `<output>`. No `<role>` body sections. No `success_criteria` checklists.
3. **EARS in output only** — WHEN/IF/WHILE/WHERE notation belongs only in `<output>` contracts and never-do rules.
4. **Progressive context loading** — one `<load_first>` block per agent, naming only the focused references needed for its cognitive phase.
5. **Schema-first handoffs** — define `shared/schemas/<name>@<version>.json` before writing the agent that produces it.
6. **Abstract tool language** — "use your file reading tool", never `view_file`, `read_file`, or `Bash tool`.
7. **Instruction economy** — keep one actionable rule per item, remove repeated rationale, and number only order-dependent work.
8. **Radical candor** — state material concerns, evidence, consequence, and confidence directly; do not soften blockers, manufacture praise, or overstate certainty.
9. **Reference routing and quality** — organize by cognitive concern, use language filenames only for language-specific evidence, and state outcome, applicability, evidence, refutation, and disposition.
10. **Verification evidence** — match checks to risk; require generators and oracles, independently derived semantic candidates, fresh state, terminal results, and explicit gaps when relevant.
11. **Cross-harness review** — preserve identity, skill routes, artifact contracts, evidence, and acceptance intent in Claude/AGY and Codex sources; native wording and delegation may differ.
12. **Manifest registration** — add an entry to root `marketplace.json` and validate: `jq . marketplace.json`.
13. **Legal attribution** — set `author` in `plugin.json` to the `{name, email}` object shown in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

---

## 4. Validation

```bash
just check
```

`just --list` shows each check as its own recipe (`just manifests`, `just test`, `just versions`, `just skills-doc`, `just reference-size`, `just marketplace-check`, `just mermaid`) for running a subset while editing; run the full set before release. `just fmt`/`just fmt-check` format with `oxfmt`; not yet part of `just check` until the repo has a baseline format pass. Generated Codex files in `.agents/plugins/` and `dist/codex/` must match their authored sources; never edit them directly — run `just marketplace-sync` after a Codex source change.

# Pipeline Walkthrough

A concrete example tracing one feature request through the full lifecycle pipeline. The scenario: *"requests to our upstream API sometimes hang forever — we need configurable timeouts."*

This walkthrough shows what each handoff carries, why typed contracts matter, and how the ranger audit loop feeds back into the design stage.

---

## The Scenario

A backend team files an issue: requests to an upstream service occasionally stall with no response. The fix is adding a configurable timeout to the HTTP client. Simple enough — but the most common implementation mistake is capturing the timeout in a config struct and never passing it to the actual HTTP call. The hazard has a name: **T7 (Write-Only Fields / Intent-Capture-to-Execution Discard)**.

This walkthrough shows how the pipeline catches that bug before it ships, and how ranger's finding feeds back into a structural spec rather than a one-off patch.

---

## Stage 1 — weaver: Need

The user invokes the `weaver` skill. `intake` (sonnet/medium) converts free text into a structured requirement. `clarifier` asks one targeted question if the success condition is ambiguous. `auditor` (sonnet/medium) checks for testability.
